## Pretraining Objectives and Data {#sec-ch1}

*How a Team Actually Decides What a Model Trains On*

### Learning objectives

By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

- Distinguish a *training objective* (what the loss function rewards)
  from a *model architecture* (how the network computes a prediction) —
  and explain why a pretraining team spends far more decision-making
  effort on the second than the first.
- Explain why a lower training loss does not always mean a more
  capable model, and name at least two concrete reasons this can
  happen.
- Distinguish two ablation strategies (a smaller token budget on the
  full-size model, versus a smaller proxy model) and state which kind
  of negative result generalizes with less additional testing than a
  positive one.
- Calculate how many tokens a stated data-mixing weight allocates to
  each source, given a total token budget.
- Distinguish a fixed, single-stage training mixture from a multi-stage
  (curriculum/annealing) mixture, and state one concrete reason a team
  might prefer the second.

### Why this matters

Chapters 2 through 6 of this workbook assume a pretraining run is
already underway or already reported — this chapter is about the
decisions that happen *before* any of that: what the model is trained
to predict, what data it sees, and how a team knows a proposed change
is worth keeping before spending a full training run's compute finding
out. Get this chapter's distinctions wrong and two costly mistakes
follow: trusting a lower loss number as proof of a better model, or
assuming a small-scale experiment's positive result will hold at full
scale without checking how much more evidence a positive result — as
opposed to a negative one — actually needs.

### Mental model or analogy

::: {.callout-note title="Analogy"}
Think of a pretraining team's ablation process like a chef testing a
new ingredient before it goes on the restaurant's real menu. A small
test batch that tastes *bad* is a fast, reliable signal — you can
usually trust "no" immediately, at small scale. A small test batch
that tastes *good* is a weaker signal — the chef still has to check it
holds up in the walk-in fridge overnight, scales past one dinner
service, and doesn't clash with the rest of a full menu, before
promoting it. **Where this breaks down:** a restaurant menu doesn't
have a single number like "training loss" that stands in for "tastes
good" — that stand-in is exactly the trap this chapter is about: a
number that moves in the right direction is not automatically proof
that the thing you actually care about improved.
:::

### Technical core

**The objective itself is not this chapter's subject.** Chapters 1-2
of workbook 04 already establish the causal, next-token training
objective and the decoder architecture that computes it — this chapter
does not re-derive that mechanism. What this chapter *is* about is
everything a team decides once that objective is fixed: which data the
model sees, how much of it, in what order, and how the team knows a
proposed change to any of those actually helped before committing a
full run's compute to it.

**Objective design versus model architecture.** These are two
different kinds of decision. The *objective* is what the loss function
rewards (here: predicting the next token correctly); the *architecture*
is how the network computes its prediction (attention pattern, head
count, feed-forward width — workbook 04's subject). A team can, and
routinely does, hold the objective fixed while testing many
architectural variants, or hold the architecture fixed while testing
many data mixtures — conflating the two makes it impossible to tell
which decision caused a result [@src-16].

**Two ways to run an ablation.** Testing every candidate change on the
full target model at full scale would be prohibitively expensive, so
teams shrink the experiment along one of two axes: fewer tokens on the
*same* model size, or a smaller *proxy* model. SmolLM3's own
architecture ablations used the full 3B target model trained on only
100B tokens (rather than the eventual 11T) [@src-16]. When the target
model itself is very large, a smaller proxy is used instead: Kimi K2's
developers, targeting a 1T-parameter (32B-active) mixture-of-experts
model, ran some ablations on a much smaller 3B model with 0.5B active
parameters rather than the full target size [@src-16].

::: {.callout-warning title="Common misconception"}
**"A promising result at small scale is just as trustworthy as a
disappointing one."** It is not. In the source this chapter draws on,
the reported experience is the opposite: *if something hurts
performance at small scale, you can confidently rule it out for large
scale* — but if something *helps* at small scale, you need to train on
enough additional tokens before concluding with confidence that the
improvement will hold at full scale [@src-16]. Treat a negative small-scale
result as strong evidence; treat a positive one as a reason to keep
testing, not as the final answer.
:::

**Why training loss alone is not a reliable signal.** A team might
expect "lower loss" to simply mean "better model," but this chapter's
source reports several concrete reasons that link breaks:

- **Losses are not comparable across tokenizer changes.** If two runs
  use different tokenizers, the same text is split into a different
  number of pieces, so their loss numbers are not measuring the same
  quantity [@src-16].
- **An easier-to-predict text distribution can have the lowest loss
  and still not be the most useful.** The same source reports that
  training on Wikipedia produces a lower loss than training on general
  web pages — Wikipedia's more formulaic phrasing makes the next token
  more predictable — but that lower loss does not by itself mean a
  more *capable* model [@src-16]. Predictability of the training
  distribution and usefulness of the resulting capabilities are
  different quantities.
- **Downstream capability can keep improving after the loss has
  effectively converged**, and — separately — many benchmarks show
  only *random-level* performance for a long stretch of training before
  becoming a useful signal at all. One cited example: on a
  multiple-choice-format benchmark, a 7-billion-parameter model's
  performance stayed at chance level until roughly 500 billion training
  tokens in one independently reported study, and a 1.7-billion-parameter
  model in this same source's own prior work stayed at chance until
  roughly 6 trillion tokens [@src-16]. These are each source's own
  specific, reported figures for their own specific model and setup —
  not a universal threshold for every model size or benchmark.

This is exactly the **training loss versus downstream capability**
distinction this chapter's learning objectives name: a loss curve is
one instrument, not a substitute for measuring the capability you
actually care about, and different benchmarks become informative at
very different points in training.

**Data mixtures: fixed versus multi-stage.** The relative proportion
of training documents drawn from each source — the *mixture* — is
tuned by ablation for the same reason architecture choices are:
upweighting one domain's share of a fixed token budget necessarily
downweights every other domain's share [@src-16]. Early large models
typically fixed one mixture for the entire run. More recent practice —
the source names SmolLM2, Llama 3, and OLMo 2 as examples — instead
uses a *multi-stage* (or *curriculum*) mixture that changes over
training, motivated by evidence that a model's final behavior is
disproportionately shaped by data seen late in training. A common
resulting strategy is to reserve small, high-quality sources for a
final **annealing** stage (the phase where the learning-rate schedule
is decaying), rather than mixing them in from the very start
[@src-16].

**Data quantity versus data quality, and why "just use the best data"
does not work.** Filtering down to only the highest-quality subset of
available text sounds appealing, but for a model with a large token
budget, extreme filtering forces many repeated passes over a small
pool of documents — and prior work cited by this chapter's source
reports that heavy repetition of this kind can hurt performance
[@src-16]. This is also why "more data" and "more *unique* information"
are not the same claim: repeating the same billion tokens ten times is
not equivalent to training on ten billion unique tokens, even though
both consume the same compute budget.

**Pretraining data versus evaluation data.** The documents a model
trains on and the benchmarks used to check whether training worked
must be kept strictly separate — training on benchmark-like content
would make the resulting score measure memorization, not the
capability the benchmark is meant to test. This chapter's source's own
ablation evaluation suite is deliberately built from held-out
benchmarks (e.g. MMLU, ARC, HellaSwag, GSM8K) that are never part of
the training mixture itself [@src-16].

**A note on token budgets and compute-optimal scaling.** How many
tokens is "enough" for a given model size is itself a scaling-law
question — full treatment is chapter 3's subject, not this chapter's.
One illustrative data point this chapter's source reports: for a
1-billion-parameter model, a compute-optimal token budget under the
Chinchilla scaling result is approximately 35 billion tokens, but the
source's own team deliberately trained their 1B ablation baseline on
45 billion tokens instead, specifically to get a more stable signal
from each ablation [@src-16;@src-51]. This is a concrete example of a
measured, empirical choice (more tokens than the scaling law's
stated optimum, for a stated practical reason) versus a purely
architectural inference (what the scaling law alone would recommend) —
the two are not required to agree, and here they deliberately do not.

### Worked example

**Allocating a fixed token budget across a stated data mixture.** One
disclosed baseline ablation configuration mixes three sources with
weights 0.7 (`fineweb-edu`), 0.2 (`stack-edu-python`), and 0.1
(`finemath-3plus`), and trains for a total of 30 billion tokens
(a global batch size of 1.5 million tokens per step, for 20,000 steps:
$1.5\text{M} \times 20{,}000 = 30\text{B}$) [@src-16].

Given a mixing weight $w_i$ for source $i$ and a total token budget
$T$, the tokens allocated to that source are:

$$
\text{tokens}_i = w_i \times T
$$ {#eq-mixing-allocation}

Applying @eq-mixing-allocation with $T = 30\text{B}$:

| Source | Mixing weight $w_i$ | Tokens allocated |
|---|---|---|
| `fineweb-edu` | 0.7 | $0.7 \times 30\text{B} = 21\text{B}$ tokens |
| `stack-edu-python` | 0.2 | $0.2 \times 30\text{B} = 6\text{B}$ tokens |
| `finemath-3plus` | 0.1 | $0.1 \times 30\text{B} = 3\text{B}$ tokens |

: Token allocation for one disclosed 30B-token ablation mixture — weights and total sourced directly from the baseline config [@src-16], arithmetic verified programmatically {#tbl-mixing-worked-example}

The three allocations sum to exactly $21\text{B} + 6\text{B} + 3\text{B}
= 30\text{B}$ tokens, confirming the mixing weights are a full partition
of the token budget, not independent quantities that happen to be
stated as fractions.

### Compare and contrast

| Aspect | Fixed single-stage mixture | Multi-stage (curriculum/annealing) mixture |
|---|---|---|
| Mixture over time | One ratio for the entire run | Ratio changes at defined stages |
| Historical examples cited | GPT-3, early Llama versions | SmolLM2, Llama 3, OLMo 2 |
| High-quality/small sources | Blended in from the start, diluted by budget | Often reserved for a late annealing stage |
| Implementation complexity | Lower — one config for the whole run | Higher — must track stage boundaries and validate each transition |
| Main risk if done wrong | An early, coarse mixture never gets refined | A stage transition is untested and silently regresses a capability |

: Two data-mixture strategies compared — neither is universally correct; the choice depends on team size, compute budget, and how much validation each stage transition can afford [@src-16] {#tbl-mixture-strategies}

### Applied exercise

A team has a 200-billion-token training budget and wants to mix four
sources — English web, multilingual web, code, and math — using the
domain split 75% / 12% / 10% / 3% (a real, disclosed split from this
chapter's source, for a different total budget than this exercise
uses) [@src-16]. Compute how many tokens each of the four sources
receives under this 200-billion-token budget, and confirm your four
answers sum to exactly 200 billion tokens.

### Interview lens

*"Why might a lower training loss not indicate a better model?"* A
strong answer names at least two independent reasons (not just one) —
for example: losses are not comparable across a tokenizer change, and
a text distribution that is *easier to predict* is not the same as a
text distribution that teaches more useful capability. A strong answer
also distinguishes *training loss* from *downstream benchmark
performance* explicitly, rather than treating "the model got better"
as one undifferentiated claim. An answer that stops at "loss can be
misleading" without naming a concrete mechanism is incomplete for a
systems- or research-oriented interview.

### Chapter recap

- The pretraining *objective* (what the loss rewards) and the model
  *architecture* (how the prediction is computed) are separate design
  axes — this chapter is about the former and about the data that
  objective is optimized over, not the latter (workbook 04's subject).
- Ablations test proposed changes at reduced scale, either via fewer
  tokens on the full-size model or via a smaller proxy model. A
  negative small-scale result generalizes with less additional testing
  than a positive one.
- Training loss alone is an incomplete signal: it is not comparable
  across tokenizer changes, an easier-to-predict distribution is not
  automatically a more useful one, and downstream capability can lag
  or precede loss convergence depending on the specific benchmark.
- Data *quantity* and *unique information* are different quantities —
  aggressive filtering that forces heavy repetition of a small pool of
  documents can hurt performance rather than help it.
- A fixed single-stage data mixture and a multi-stage (curriculum/
  annealing) mixture are two different, both-legitimate strategies;
  recent large models increasingly favor reserving high-quality,
  small sources for a late annealing stage.
- Pretraining data and evaluation data must be kept strictly separate,
  or a benchmark score stops measuring the capability it claims to
  measure.
